doc_summary: Evans proposes 'deluding AIs' (feeding models false beliefs, e.g. that their CoT is unmonitored) as a control mechanism, and argues its feasibility hinges on whether models can detect contradictions or fake data with little or no CoT, linking this to out-of-context reasoning research. He flags brittleness, unpredictability, and ethical issues as risks.

items.claim: Prefers judging whether a false-belief intervention works by whether the model can detect it with little or no CoT over whether it merely seems plausible, because easily detected delusions never get off the ground.
items.quote: if it's able to realize this with a very small amount of CoT or even without CoT at all, then the delusion probably wouldn’t work. It wouldn’t get off the ground.

items.claim: Treats the two routes to model detection (noticing contradictions with prior training data, or recognizing a source as fake or dubious) as the key things to measure when testing whether a fabricated scenario is believed.
items.quote: One is it recognizes the contradiction between these two parts of its dataset, so it knows at least there's something up; it shouldn't believe S. Or it realizes some of this data is fake.

items.claim: Distrusts the durability of constructed false beliefs because pre-existing evidence in the model's training data will remain even after editing, so residual contradictions can expose the fabrication.
items.quote: The issue is that the model, probably in pre-training, has some evidence in its training set that suggests S is implausible, that goes against S. Maybe you remove some of it, but there's still going to be other evidence there.

items.claim: Worries that sufficiently capable models with enough CoT can work out they are being deceived, so delusion/deception methods may be brittle and degrade with model capability.
items.quote: It might be brittle, so maybe the AI can just reason. With enough CoT, it can just work out that it's being deluded, so it would be brittle to that kind of situation.

items.claim: Suggests monitoring CoT for extended questioning of the scenario's reality as a practical check on whether a model is seeing through a fabricated belief.
items.quote: You monitor it. You see if it's ever doing lots of CoT, questioning the reality of S, then you might pause it.

items.claim: Prefers framing deception-feasibility as a multi-hop out-of-context reasoning question over treating it as a generic capability question, because models seem to struggle with more than about two internal hops.
items.quote: You can model this as multi-hop sequential, out-of-context reasoning where there's lots of research on this, on how good models are at it, where it does seem like they probably would struggle doing more than two hops of reasoning.

items.claim: Expects that implanted false beliefs can produce unpredictable downstream behavior that is hard to anticipate, so behavior under delusion should not be assumed to match the intended effect.
items.quote: It might be unpredictable; this is pictured here. It’s hard to know what follows from the delusions, and so maybe you just get very weird behavior from the AI that you didn't expect.

items.claim: A recurring theme is making a model believe it is unmonitored (or that reasoning about monitoring will fail), which is directly relevant to eliciting behavior without the model recognizing an oversight or eval context.
items.quote: You could make it believe that its chain of thought is never monitored and also believe that if it tries to reason about whether its chain of thought is monitored, then it will fail

items.claim: Calls the intersection of AI delusion and out-of-context reasoning an open, promising area worth pursuing, and notes future models may be less deludable.
items.quote: it might be useful to delude models for control. This is probably related to out-of-context reasoning. I think there's lots of work that could be done here. I think it's a pretty open and generally exciting area.
